> **What you can defend when you leave.** Turn a curiosity into a question whose answer you could recognize, and say what kind of answer it would be.

## What this studio produces

An objective, your units, outcomes and conditions, your target and reach, and a provisional claim boundary.

This is a **versioned checkpoint**, not a pass. You date it, number it, and
attach the reason for the version. When later evidence changes it, you write
the next version rather than editing the last one, because the sequence of
changes is itself part of your research record.

## The lessons in this studio

- [Lesson 5 — From Curiosity to a Research Problem](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part2-curiosity-to-design/05-from-curiosity-to-a-research-problem.html)
- [Lesson 6 — Descriptive, Predictive, and Causal Questions](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part2-curiosity-to-design/06-descriptive-predictive-and-causal-questions.html)

They follow this page. Read them in order, doing each lesson's **It is your
turn** as you go, and then come back here: the studio is where those pieces
become one artifact you can defend.

## The practice {#checkpoint}

1. State your objective in one sentence a stranger could repeat back.
2. Name your units, your outcome, and the conditions you are comparing or describing.
3. Declare kind and reach, and write the words in your question that fix each one.
4. Write your provisional claim boundary: the sentence you hope to defend, and the sentence you will not be able to.

## The four rails, here

Four concerns cross every studio in this book. At this studio they take
these specific forms.

- **Ethics, permissions, and data exposure.** Note whether answering this question requires people, and flag it now.
- **Evidence, provenance, and reproducibility.** Nothing here is settled until Studio 3 checks it against what is already known.
- **AI activity, verification, and human decisions.** If AI helped shape the question, the ledger records what you kept and what you rejected.
- **Uncertainty, claim boundary, and revision history.** A question with no recognizable answer cannot carry uncertainty; fix the question first.

## What sends you back

Studio 3 almost always sends you back here. That is the design, not a setback.

## How this checkpoint is assessed

Each row scores **0**, **1**, or **2**. **10 points total.**

| # | Criterion | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The station's artifact exists in full, specific to your own project | absent, or generic text that would fit any project | present but incomplete, or specific in some parts and generic in others | complete and unmistakably about your project |
| 2 | The checkpoint is written as a dated, numbered version with its reason | no version, or a version with no reason given | versioned, but the reason is decorative rather than an account of what changed | versioned with a reason a reader could use to reconstruct your thinking |
| 3 | Every judgment in the artifact is defended by you, not asserted by a tool | conclusions appear with no reasoning, or reproduce a tool's wording | reasoning present but thin where the decision was hardest | each judgment carries a reason you could defend under questioning |
| 4 | The four rails are carried in this station's specific form | one or more rails absent where this station required them | all rails present but one is nominal | every rail addressed in the form this station requires |
| 5 | The station's own product is present and defensible: An objective, your units, outcomes and conditions, your target and reach, and a provisional claim boundary | the station's own product is missing | present but would not survive a careful question | present and defensible as stated |
